title: The quake has already started, so how can the alert get there first? | So That's Why
description:
Little Q is eating breakfast when Mom's phone suddenly screams; only a few seconds later does the house start to shake. How could the phone know before the earthquake? Is it predicting earthquakes?

In this episode, the Chief and Little Q picture an earthquake as a race that starts underground: the little messenger (the P wave), which runs fast and shakes gently; the big guy (the S wave), which runs slowly and shakes hard; the stations by the track that hear the little messenger; and the earthquake alert, which rides on electricity and outruns the big guy. We also see why places right next to the epicenter often get too little warning, and why, in the big 2024 Hualien earthquake, Taipei shook hard but phones stayed silent.

An earthquake alert is not a prediction: once an earthquake has already started, a computer estimates it from the earliest data, so the estimate can be off and the alert can come too late. If you hear an alert or feel shaking, Drop, Cover, and Hold On right away; don't wait for your phone.

The illustrations in this episode were made with AI; they are diagrams, not measurements. The speeds and seconds in the video are approximate figures from Taiwan's Central Weather Administration and from research, a few are our own rough math, and every earthquake is different. The source of every claim is listed in the references below.

Information as of 2026-11-07
